absent: Implementation of embedding and page first chunk allocators and unit offset layout.
Numeric locality distance values and early node mapping behavior.
Global descriptor table entry format and per processor slot index.
Floating point lock behavior and processor register access semantics.
Shadow stack allocator behavior and shadow memory region management.
Floating point frame reservation and copy routines plus protection key semantics.
Restartable sequence cleanup and alternate stack helper behavior.
Thirty two bit gateway image layout and signal return stub mechanics.
Signal mask saving and compatibility conversion details.
Node to mask construction and sibling mask use after boot.

findings.text: Early boot service that creates per processor storage for every possible processor and leaves it ready for later use, including offset initialization and supporting maps.
Small helper that ensures the page mapping for one per processor address exists by delegating to the extra mapping facility.
Boot time helper that allocates the mask used to track sibling setup during processor bringup.
User shadow stack adjusters that read or store one entry while moving the user shadow stack pointer, gated on the shadow stack feature being active for the task.
Signal path helpers that extend the user shadow stack on signal entry with bookkeeping plus handler return location, and later validate and restore the prior pointer on signal return.
System call that validates requested address size and option flags, aligns size to page granularity, checks for overflow and low address misuse, then delegates to the shadow stack allocator.
Small shadow stack utilities that report whether the feature is active and overwrite the entry at the current user pointer when active.

Signal delivery dispatcher that first performs restartable sequence cleanup for the interrupted context, then selects the classic thirty two bit, extended thirty two bit, or sixty four bit frame builder based on frame kind.
Thirty two bit signal frame builders for classic and real time forms that place signal number, context, mask, and return information on the user stack and prepare user registers for handler entry.

Sixty four bit real time frame builder that requires an explicit user restorer, creates user context with alternate stack and mask, integrates shadow stack handling, and sets handler argument registers plus code and stack selectors.

Boot time entries run once during early initialization to establish per processor areas and sibling masks, while the shadow stack mapper and signal frame builders serve as user reachable and signal delivery entries after boot.

Distance query reports a local value when two processors map to the same early locality node and a remote value otherwise, collapsing to always local when locality support is absent, with node lookup simply forwarding to the early mapping.

Per processor allocation prefers the embedding approach unless page mode is chosen, with thirty two bit locality builds defaulting to page mode, using a large block alignment on sixty four bit and a small page alignment on thirty two bit, retrying with the page approach after a logged warning and halting boot if both approaches fail.

Each processor offset is formed from a common delta between the allocated base and the linked per processor start plus a per unit displacement, with identity and self offset fields initialized alongside, and the boot processor reloading global table and base state after its own values change.

Early translation tables for local interrupt identity, firmware identity, and locality placement are copied into per processor storage for every possible processor, early table pointers are then cleared to mark the static arrays as going away, and node to mask plus local masks are built before resynchronizing the initial page table so the new mappings are visible to low level boot code.
On thirty two bit builds each processor gets a per processor segment entry in its own global table whose base tracks that processor offset and whose limit spans the full segment range.

Reads and updates of the user shadow stack pointer always occur while holding the floating point register lock with state loaded, and push or pop first verify task level enablement before touching the pointer register.

Signal tokens stored on the shadow stack are tagged with a high marker bit to separate them from genuine return addresses, with stores rejecting payloads that already carry the marker and loads rejecting entries that lack it.

Token push requires an aligned target pointer and reserves one frame before writing the tagged value, while token pop requires an aligned current pointer, confirms the memory belongs to a shadow stack region with protection against concurrent mapping changes, then checks alignment and user range of the restored pointer before adopting it.

Signal entry obtains the current user pointer, rejects an empty value, pushes a token frame, then pushes the user restorer address and publishes the new pointer, while signal return reads the pointer, pops and validates the token, and publishes the restored pointer, with both directions becoming a no operation when hardware or task enablement is missing.
Shadow stack mapping rejects unsupported hardware, unknown option bits, undersized token requests, low addresses when a hint is supplied, and size alignment overflow before allocation.

Frame kind tests combine build time availability with per signal action flags to distinguish classic thirty two bit compatibility, native thirty two bit, and thirty two bit extended handling from the default sixty four bit path.

Signal stack preparation saves the current protection key rights value and then clears it to permit access, with callers restoring the saved value after floating point state has been copied or on copy failure.

Frame placement starts from the interrupted stack pointer, reserves the sixty four bit red zone when applicable, switches to the alternate stack or legacy restorer stack when conditions hold, reserves floating point state, subtracts the frame size, applies ABI specific alignment, rejects overflow of an engaged alternate stack with a deliberately invalid address plus a rate limited notice, and only then copies floating point state under relaxed protection keys.

Maximum signal frame size is computed once at boot from the largest signal context size plus alignment slack plus default floating point state size plus extra save padding, rounded up to frame alignment and reported through the log.

Classic and real time thirty two bit builders select a user restorer from the signal action or from the thirty two bit gateway image with a stack fallback, store signal identity context mask and return code, and enter the handler with stack and instruction pointers plus legacy argument registers and user data and thirty two bit code selectors, cleaning up the user access window on any fault.

The sixty four bit builder fails when no user restorer is supplied, otherwise writes context flags with cleared link plus alternate stack and return address plus context plus mask, copies extended signal information when requested, integrates shadow stack setup, and enters the handler with signal number and info and context pointers plus cleared accumulator and sixty four bit code selector while preserving or repairing the stack selector.

Stack selector repair inspects the interrupted selector with a processor attributes query and only keeps selectors that denote user privilege readable and writable present data, replacing anything else with the standard user data selector.

User context flags always mark shadow stack context, add extended save state when the boot processor supports it, and add strict stack selector restoration when the interrupted context is in sixty four bit mode.
Unsafe context and mask helpers delegate to low level setup routines and jump to a caller supplied fault label on failure, keeping the user access window handling in the caller.
Log output from the signal module is prefixed with the module name followed by a separator, as established by the file local format macro.
User shadow stack pointer register access is serialized by acquiring the floating point lock with state loaded and releasing it afterwards, covering reads, pushes, pops, and signal transitions.

Token pop holds the memory map read lock only to locate and classify the containing region plus capture a speculation sequence, releases it before reading the tagged value from user memory, and retries if the mapping changed during the read.

Signal frame stores run inside a user access window that is explicitly opened before the first store and closed on both success and fault paths, with faults converging on a single cleanup label that closes the window and reports a memory fault.

Observed thirty two bit and sixty four bit signal frames carry signal identity, handler return location, saved processor context, alternate stack description, and signal mask, with real time forms adding info and context pointers plus flags and link.

Per processor bringup moves from allocator selection through fallback and failure halt, to offset derivation and per processor field init, to early table copy and invalidation, to mask construction, ending with page table resynchronization.

Shadow stack signal handling moves from idle to token plus restorer pushed on delivery, remaining there across handler execution, then back to restored pointer after validation on return, with any validation failure aborting the transition.

Signal frame creation moves from stack selection through floating point reservation and alignment, to overflow rejection, to protected state copy, to user frame stores, to register and selector preparation for handler entry.
Boot halts if no per processor allocation strategy succeeds, and low memory allocation failures or mapping gaps can leave early mappings unavailable to secondary processor entry code.

Shadow stack operations fail safely on missing enablement, unaligned pointers, non shadow stack regions, missing marker bits, out of range restore values, user memory faults, interrupted mapping locks, and undersized or overflowing allocation requests.

Signal delivery fails safely with a memory fault on user access faults, alternate stack overflow, missing sixty four bit restorer, or shadow stack setup failure, and repairs a bogus stack selector rather than entering the handler with an invalid value.
Each shadow stack slot occupies eight bytes.
Signal frames observe sixteen byte stack alignment with up to fifteen bytes of padding.
Extra save area reservation for signal frames allows up to sixty three bytes of padding.
Shadow stack data marker uses bit sixty three of a sixty four bit slot.
Worst case signal info plus context size is bounded by the thirty two bit frame on thirty two bit builds and by the sixty four bit real time frame otherwise.
